A **condensation** polymer is formed when monomers join with the **loss of a small molecule**,
usually water. An **addition** polymer is formed when monomers simply add together, with
nothing eliminated.
**(c) Dacron** ✓ — a **polyester**, made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid:
n HOCH₂CH₂OH + n HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH ⟶ [–OCH₂CH₂OOC–C₆H₄–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
Water is eliminated at every link, so this is a **condensation** polymer ✓ (Dacron is also
sold as Terylene, and as PET it is the plastic of drink bottles.)
The other three are all **addition** polymers of a single alkene monomer, formed without
losing anything:
**(a) PVC** — from vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl
**(b) Teflon** — from tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂
**(d) Polystyrene** — from styrene, C₆H₅CH=CH₂
Two quick tests distinguish the classes. An addition polymer has the **same empirical formula
as its monomer**, since nothing is lost; a condensation polymer does not. And addition
polymers come from monomers with a **C=C double bond**, while condensation polymers come from
monomers with **two functional groups** each — two –OH, two –COOH, two –NH₂ — which is what
lets the chain grow at both ends.
∴ Dacron.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|8|Pradeep Chemistry:
Three statements are correct and one is not.
**(a) Fibres possess high tensile strength** ✓ **true.** Fibres such as nylon and Terylene
have **strong intermolecular forces** — hydrogen bonds between the amide or ester groups of
neighbouring chains. The chains pack closely and crystallise, which is exactly what gives
high tensile strength and very little stretch.
**(b) Thermoplastic polymers soften on heating and harden on cooling, repeatedly** ✓ **true.**
Polythene, PVC and polystyrene have **linear or lightly branched** chains held only by weak
intermolecular forces. Heating lets the chains slide past one another, so the material can be
moulded again and again.
**(d) Elastomers have polymer chains held together by weak intermolecular forces** ✓ **true.**
That weakness, together with the coiled chains, is what makes rubber stretch and spring back.
**(c) Thermosetting polymers are reusable** ✗ **not correct** — this is the answer.
Thermosetting polymers such as **bakelite, melamine and urea-formaldehyde** are **heavily
cross-linked**: on first heating, covalent bonds form between the chains and lock them into a
rigid three-dimensional network. That network cannot be melted or remoulded. Heat them again
and they **char and decompose** rather than soften.
The practical consequence is familiar: a polythene bag can be recycled by melting, a bakelite
switch cannot.
∴ statement (c).

**Cationic polymerisation** proceeds through a growing **carbocation**, so the initiator must
be something that can generate a positive charge on the monomer — that is, a **Lewis acid**,
an electron-pair acceptor.
**(b) AlCl₃** ✓ — a classic Lewis acid. With a trace of water or HCl as co-catalyst it
generates a proton or an AlCl₃-complexed ion, which adds to the alkene and leaves a
carbocation at the far end. That cation attacks the next monomer, and the chain grows.
BF₃ and SnCl₄ work the same way; BF₃ with isobutylene is the industrial route to butyl rubber.
The others initiate quite different mechanisms, or none:
**(c) BuLi** ✗ — butyllithium is a powerful **carbanion** source and initiates **anionic**
polymerisation, the opposite kind. It is used for styrene and dienes.
**(d) LiAlH₄** ✗ — a **reducing agent**, a hydride donor. It would attack a monomer rather
than start a chain.
**(a) HNO₃** ✗ — a Brønsted acid and oxidant, not a Lewis acid of the right sort, and it would
oxidise or nitrate the monomer rather than initiate polymerisation.
The three mechanisms are worth keeping apart by their initiators: **peroxides or AIBN** for
free-radical, **Lewis acids** for cationic, and **organolithiums or amides** for anionic. The
monomer decides which is feasible: electron-rich alkenes such as isobutylene go cationic,
electron-poor ones such as acrylonitrile go anionic.
∴ AlCl₃.

Nylon is a **polyamide** ✓ — a polymer whose repeating link is the **amide** group,
**–CO–NH–**.
Nylon-6,6 is made by condensing a diamine with a dicarboxylic acid, losing water at each
link:
n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH ⟶ [–NH(CH₂)₆NH–CO(CH₂)₄CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
and the '6,6' records the six carbons in each monomer.
Nylon-6 is made differently, from the single monomer **caprolactam**, but the repeating link
is again an amide, so it too is a polyamide.
The amide group is what gives nylon its properties. Neighbouring chains **hydrogen-bond**
through their –CO–NH– groups, pack closely and crystallise, which is why nylon is a strong,
tough **fibre** with high tensile strength and very little stretch.
It is also why nylon resembles **protein** chemically — proteins are natural polyamides, with
the same –CO–NH– peptide link. Both are hydrolysed by hot acid back to their monomers.
The other options belong to other classes:
**(b) polythene** — an addition polymer of ethene, a pure hydrocarbon
**(c) polyester** — the Dacron/Terylene class, with **–COO–** links instead of amide
**(d) polysaccharide** — a natural polymer of sugars, such as starch or cellulose
∴ polyamide.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|18|Pradeep Chemistry:
Look for the polymer whose repeating unit contains a **nitrogen atom**.
**(c) Nylon** ✓ — a **polyamide**, whose repeating link is **–CO–NH–**. The nitrogen is part
of the backbone of the chain, so nylon is unmistakably a nitrogen-containing polymer ✓
The others contain none:
**(a) Polyvinyl chloride**, [–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ — carbon, hydrogen and **chlorine** only
**(d) Terylene** (Dacron), a **polyester** — carbon, hydrogen and **oxygen** only, with the
repeating –COO– ester link
**(b) Bakelite** — a phenol-formaldehyde resin, again carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. (The
related **melamine**-formaldehyde resin *does* contain nitrogen, which is why bakelite is a
tempting distractor for anyone who confuses the two.)
The presence of nitrogen in nylon is not incidental — it is what makes the polymer useful.
The –NH– of one chain hydrogen-bonds to the C=O of the next, and that hydrogen bonding holds
the chains together strongly enough to give a high-tensile fibre.
Other nitrogen-containing polymers worth knowing are **polyacrylonitrile** (Orlon, with a
–CN group on each unit), **melamine-formaldehyde** and the **proteins**, which are nature's
own polyamides.
∴ nylon.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|21|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Orlon**, also sold as **Acrilan**, is **polyacrylonitrile** ✓ — the addition polymer of
acrylonitrile:
n CH₂=CH–CN ⟶ **[–CH₂–CH(CN)–]ₙ**
The polymerisation is a free-radical addition, usually initiated by a peroxide.
Each repeating unit carries a **–CN group**, and those strongly polar nitrile groups attract
one another between neighbouring chains. That dipole-dipole attraction holds the chains
closely together and is what makes Orlon a **fibre** rather than a soft plastic: it is
strong, resistant to chemicals and to sunlight, and it does not absorb much water.
Its practical use follows: Orlon is the usual **substitute for wool**, used in sweaters,
blankets and carpets, because it is warm, light and does not shrink or attract moths.
The other options are different classes of polymer:
**(a) cellulose** — a natural polysaccharide, the material of cotton and of rayon
**(c) polyamide** — the nylon class, with –CO–NH– links
**(d) polyesters** — the Dacron/Terylene class, with –COO– links
Acrylonitrile is also one half of two important **copolymers**: with butadiene and styrene it
gives **ABS** plastic, and with butadiene alone it gives **Buna-N**, the oil-resistant
synthetic rubber.
∴ polyacrylonitrile.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|22|Pradeep Chemistry:
Addition polymerisation of two different alkenes gives a **copolymer** in which the two
monomer units **alternate** along a chain built entirely of –CH₂–CH– repeat units. Nothing is
lost, and no new skeleton is created — the double bonds simply open up and join end to end.
**The monomers:**
styrene, CH₂=CH–**C₆H₅**
acrylonitrile, CH₂=CH–**CN**
**Opening each double bond** turns CH₂=CH–X into –CH₂–CH(X)–, and joining them alternately
gives
**[–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–CH₂–CH(CN)–]ₙ** ✓ — which is option (d)
Notice the pattern: a **–CH₂– then a substituted CH, then another –CH₂– then the other
substituted CH**. Every substituent sits on **alternate** carbons, because each monomer
contributes two carbons and carries its group on the second one.
The distractors break that pattern in instructive ways:
**(a)** places two –CH₂– groups next to each other and the substituents on adjacent carbons
**(c)** puts the phenyl and the nitrile on **neighbouring** carbons, which would need the
monomers to join head-to-head
**(b)** invents an extra methyl group that neither monomer supplies
The quickest check is to count: the repeat unit must contain **four** carbons in the
backbone, two from each monomer, with the substituents on the 2nd and 4th.
This copolymer, **SAN**, is a rigid transparent plastic, and adding butadiene to the same
pair gives **ABS**.
∴ option (d).
